resources.string: ScrollMeter measures how far content moves on the screen while you scroll and turns it into metres. The service receives only scroll events: numbers about the movement and the name of the app. It does not read text, messages or screen content, controls nothing and sends no data anywhere — the app has no internet access.

resources.string: How far do you scroll every day?
ScrollMeter measures how far content moves on the screen while you scroll — in social apps, in the browser and elsewhere — and shows it in metres and kilometres.
Screen time tells you how long. ScrollMeter shows you how far.
When you scroll, Android reports how many pixels the content moved. ScrollMeter adds that up and turns it into a length using the pixel size of your display.
What is measured is the movement of the content, not what is on the screen: ScrollMeter does not know what you read or write — only how far it moved.
The glide after a flick counts too, so the distance is usually longer than your finger’s path.
Some apps do not report scrolling (YouTube, for example) — ScrollMeter measures nothing in them.
ScrollMeter needs access to the Accessibility service so that Android tells the app about scrolling in other apps.
ScrollMeter uses only scroll events and the name of the app in which the scrolling happened.
It does not read or store screen text, messages, passwords or form contents.
The data is processed and stored only on this device.
I understand and want to continue

In the settings that open, find ScrollMeter (usually under “Downloaded apps” or “Installed apps”) and turn it on. Android shows a general warning about what accessibility services may do — ScrollMeter uses only scroll events.

If Android says “Restricted setting”: open Settings › Apps › ScrollMeter, choose “Allow restricted settings” in the ⋮ menu at the top right and try again. This applies to apps installed outside the Play Store.
If you force stop ScrollMeter in the app settings, Android turns measuring off. Turn it on again here or on the overview.

ScrollMeter converts pixels to millimetres using what the display reports about itself. Calibrating with a payment card is more accurate: you hold it against the display and match a line to its length. It takes about a minute and can also be done later in Settings › Measurement accuracy.
The display is already calibrated with a payment card.
ScrollMeter can add to the distance how much time you spend in each app.
For that it needs “Usage access”. ScrollMeter reads from the system when which app was in the foreground and stores only the total minutes per app and day. None of it leaves the phone.
It does not read app content, messages or browser history. You can remove the permission any time in the Android settings.
Without it ScrollMeter keeps measuring — time in apps just shows “—”.
In the settings that open, find ScrollMeter and turn on “Permit usage access”.
Tap a bar to open that day.
This app reports standard Android scroll data and the display is calibrated, so the measurement is probably reliable.
The measurement is usable, but either the display is not calibrated with a card or the app often reports only a position instead of a movement.
Many events from this app carry no usable movement, so the measured distance is likely lower than the real one.
There are not enough events from this app to judge yet.
You scroll %1$s of %2$s in the app (%3$s %%).
This app does not report scrolling — ScrollMeter only knows the time spent in it.
E.g. “That is about one lap of a running track.”
Once a day, when you go over your daily limit.
With the first scroll of the day: how much it was yesterday.
Notifications for ScrollMeter are off in the system, so none will arrive.
A limit is not a target but a line you do not want to cross in a day. The colour shows how close you are: green, orange from %1$d %%, red over the limit. Nothing is blocked.
Enter a number from 10 m to 100 km.

per_app.csv has a row for every day and app: distance, event counts and time in app. daily_summary.csv has the total for every day. Excluded apps are not in them. The files are created on the phone; where you save them or whom you send them to is up to you.
The export did not work. Try again.
This deletes the history, app totals, time in apps and the records of individual scrolls. It cannot be undone.
Not everything could be deleted. Try again.
The setting could not be saved. Try again.
An excluded app is no longer measured and disappears from all totals, the history and the export. When you switch it back on, its earlier data returns.
Name not available (app without a home screen icon)
ScrollMeter uses the accessibility service only to detect scroll events. It does not read or store text, messages, passwords or screen content. The measured data stays on the phone.
It stores only: when scrolling happened, in which app (package name), how many pixels the content moved and the distance calculated from that.
It never reads or stores: text, messages, passwords, web addresses, screen content, filled-in forms or user names.
ScrollMeter reads from the system when which app was in the foreground and stores only the total minutes per app and day. None of it leaves the phone.
The app has no internet permission: it sends nothing and has no account, ads or analytics. Data leaves the phone only through an export you start yourself, and you delete it in Settings › Data.
The data is not backed up to the cloud or moved to a new phone. To take it along, use Export CSV.

Why the Accessibility service: otherwise Android does not tell an app how far the content of another app moved. The service listens only to the “scrolled” event and has no permission to read window content.
The movement Android reports while scrolling (scrollDeltaX/Y, otherwise the change of position), converted to millimetres using the physical pixel size of this display.

Put a payment card against the display and use the slider to make the blue line as long as the card’s longer side.
Place the card upright right next to the blue line, its top edge on the top mark. Fine-tune the bottom mark with − and +.
A longer line does not fit here. Hold the phone upright.
An automatic estimate from what the display reports about itself. Calibrating with a payment card is more accurate.

A new calibration applies only to newly measured data. Distances already measured are not recalculated.
